turns.question: Why did node inserts under a unique constraint get so slow in 6.0.0, and who fixed it?
turns.text:
**Why it was slow:** In 6.0.0 the Rust constraint check rebuilt a hash of every key in the label once for each entity written. A commit therefore cost O(written × label size). A single `CREATE` cost O(label), and bulk inserts were quadratic [2]. The reporter measured 20,000 nodes taking 36 s on 6.0.0, against 307 ms on 4.20.7 for the last 10,000 [1]. Without the constraint, the same insert took 26 ms [1].

**Who fixed it:** AviAvni authored PR #3334. It was merged and closes issue #3330 [2]. The fix looks each written entity up in the constraint's supporting index, as the C `EnforceUniqueEntity` does. Entities written in the same commit are compared through a key set. If there is no operational index, or the value can't be matched exactly, the label is scanned once per commit instead of once per entity [2]. In the author's benchmark, inserting nodes 10,001–20,000 went from about 26,047 ms to 20 ms [2].

**Related work:** alblancc's earlier PR #3225 took the same index-lookup approach for #2995. It was closed for now because it depends on #3086 and #3098 [3]. The issue was reported by jasperblues [1].

turns.question: Why did wrapping a WHERE predicate in parentheses stop the query from using the index?
turns.text:
The parser's parenthesis node was reaching the optimizer and hiding the predicate from the index passes. Results stayed correct; only the plan got worse. This happened in the Rust implementation (reported as a 6.0.0 regression) [1][2].

- **Cause:** The parser keeps an `ExprIR::Paren` node for `( ... )` because it needs it while parsing. The binder copied that node into the bound tree. The optimizer passes (`utilize_index`, `utilize_node_by_id`, filter push-down, Cartesian-to-hash-join) match on the filter root and on the children of a top-level `And`. A `Paren` wrapper hid the predicate from all of them [1].
- **Effect:** `WHERE (n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1)` used a Node By Label Scan instead of a Node By Index Scan. `WHERE (id(n) = 42)` used All Node Scan plus Filter instead of NodeByIdSeek [1][2][3].
- **Fix:** PR #3335 changed the binder (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs`) so it drops the `Paren` wrapper. It also merges a nested `And` or `Or` into a parent of the same operator, so `(a AND b) AND c` splits into three conjuncts. No optimizer pass needs to know about parentheses [1].

turns.question: Why did batch-backport skip some of the PRs it should have backported?
turns.text:
The batch-backport workflow dropped PRs because of how it searched for them (issue #3191) [1]:

- **No paging:** It found PRs with one call to the GitHub search API. The call set no page size and didn't page. The API returns 30 results per page by default, so a run backported at most 30 PRs and dropped the rest without listing them [1]. For example, the 6.0 run on 2026-10-08 matched 44 PRs but opened #3189 with only 30. The other 14 were cherry-picked in by hand [1].
- **Date-only filter:** The search filtered on the tag's date rather than its time (`merged:>YYYY-MM-DD`). That leaves out PRs merged later on the day the tag was made [1].

PR #3192 fixed the paging. The search now asks for 100 results per page and reads every page [2]. The snippet I read doesn't say whether the date-versus-time filter was also fixed.

- Inserting nodes 10,001–20,000 took 307 ms on 4.20.7 and 36,280 ms on 6.0.0.
- Without the constraint, 20,000 nodes took 26 ms on 6.0.0, so the constraint check was the slow part.

Where the index can't match a value exactly, or no operational index exists, it scans the label once per commit instead of once per entity [2]. turns.question: Why does our container image stop launching its server process with administrator privileges?
turns.text:
The runtime image used to run `redis-server` as root. Issue #3180 asked to run it as a dedicated unprivileged `falkordb` user instead, "the way the official redis image runs it as `redis`" [1]. PR #3181 implemented this and closes that issue [2]. The graph doesn't state a deeper rationale, such as a specific security incident.

How it works now:
- `run.sh` starts as root and hands the data directory and the generated TLS certificates to `falkordb`. It then execs `redis-server` through `gosu`, so the server stays PID 1 [1][2].
- The image creates a `falkordb` account (uid/gid 999) in place of the old `redis` account [1].
- The container still stays root when started with `--user`, when it lacks CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID, or when `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1` is set. `SKIP_FIX_PERMS=1` skips the ownership step [1][2].

So the server only drops privileges when the container starts as root with those capabilities. In those cases the process is not launched with administrator privileges.

turns.question: What crashed everything when logging a lengthy query containing accented characters?
turns.text:
The crash was a panic in the Rust engine's slow log (issue #3233). The slow log truncates query text at byte 2048. When a multi-byte character such as `é` straddled that byte, the cut landed in the middle of the character. The slow log then panicked and killed the whole server [1].

The C module doesn't panic on the same input. It stores the first 2048 bytes plus `...`, which leaves the `é` cut in half and the stored text invalid UTF-8. The same thing happens with long `CYPHER p='...é...'` parameter strings [1].

PR #3234 fixed it. Slow-log entries now truncate long query text and CYPHER parameter values at valid character boundaries, and truncated values end with an ellipsis [2].

turns.question: What happened when someone asked for an enormous number of nearest neighbours by similarity?
turns.text:
In the Rust engine, a huge `k` in `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` crashed the server. It was reported as issue #3085 [1].

- **Cause:** `Graph::vector_query_nodes` and `vector_query_edges` built their output with `Vec::with_capacity(k)`, using the user's `k`. With `k = 10^15` the allocation aborted and killed the server [2].
- **Second problem:** The unclamped `k` was also passed to the KNN query. With `k = i64::MAX`, that query returned no rows, whereas the C engine returns every entity in both cases [2].
- **Fix:** PR #3088 (by AviAvni, merged) sizes the output by the candidates actually returned. It also clamps `k` to the graph's node count, or relationship count for edges, before building the query. That count is an O(1) upper bound on the index size, so results don't change for any `k` that was already valid [2].
- **Test:** The new flow test `test11_huge_k_is_clamped` runs `k = 10^15` and `k = i64::MAX`. It asserts that all 1001 nodes come back and that the server still answers PING. Before the fix the server crashed ("process is not alive") [2].

turns.question: How do I profile FalkorDB to find where a query spends its time?
turns.text:
The repo's profile skill describes two ways to profile. One is for a workload you drive yourself. The other uses the benchmark harness.

**1. Flamegraphs with samply (for query-execution bottlenecks)** [1]
```bash
cargo install samply        # one-time
RUSTFLAGS="-C debuginfo=2" cargo build --release
samply record redis-server --loadmodule ./target/release/libfalkordb.dylib   # libfalkordb.so on Linux
```
- A plain `--release` build has no line info, because `debug` is commented out in `[profile.release]`. That is why debuginfo is added. [1]
- Run your query or workload against the server, then stop it. samply then opens the Firefox Profiler UI. [1]
- The skill points to `docs/profiling.md` for the full reference. I did not open that file. [1]

**2. Benchmark harness (`bench/`)** [1][2]
- Build with `cargo build --release`, then run `uv run --project bench bench measure`. This records per-query instructions, cycles, allocated bytes and wall-clock time. [2]
- `bench compare` checks the results against your own baseline. [1][2]
- To drill into one hot query, run `bench profile "<query name>"`. It records the server with samply while that query runs in a loop. [1][2]
- Linux needs PMU access for `perf stat`. [2]

**In CI:** label a PR `benchmark-cov`. It compares the PR with its base per query and adds callgrind instruction counts. [1]
